query: Starting from bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what single intervention could further reduce its lattice contribution to thermal conductivity relative to the unchanged material? Earlier studies examined heat transport in idealized fcc and bcc concentrated alloys using atomistic calculations, DFT coupled to analytical models, or Debye-based estimates. Most simulations treated perfect, defect-free bulk crystals, while experiments below 200 K inferred separate lattice and electronic contributions from thermal-conductivity and electrical-resistivity measurements. For HfNbTaTiZr, these contributions were estimated to have similar magnitudes from nearly 0 to 200 K; measurements from 300 to 1200 K instead concern a sample containing 1 wt.% oxygen, limiting direct comparison with the starting material. Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its physical mechanism, a quantitative or directional prediction relative to unchanged bulk HfNbTaTiZr, the temperature and material-state boundaries of the prediction, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that would falsify the hypothesis while separating lattice-mediated from electronic heat transport.

revised_generation.hypothesis: Introducing lattice defects through 3D ink-extrusion printing and silicide coating can reduce the lattice contribution to thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr
revised_generation.mechanism: Depressed electron/phonon propagation due to distorted lattice structure and many lattice defects
revised_generation.baseline: Thermal conductivity of pure Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr
revised_generation.uncertainty: Low thermal conductivity has been reported in a high-entropy Al 0.3 CoCrFeNi alloy, but the exact mechanism is not fully understood
revised_generation.falsification_experiment: Measure the thermal conductivity of 3D ink-extrusion printed and silicide coated HfNbTaTiZr and compare it to the thermal conductivity of pure Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr

3D Ink‐Extrusion Printing

The 3D ink extrusion printing, sintering, and silicide coating processes are shown in Figure 1 a . The ≈410 µm filaments containing metallic/hydride powders are printed layer by layer to produce complex parts, including a lattice sandwich structure, as shown in Figure 1b . When the filaments are extruded, the solvent (dichloromethane, DCM) evaporates near‐instantaneously, and the binder (polystyrene, PS) precipitates, leading to a quick increase in the strength of filaments that helps the structure to self‐support. After sintering, these samples are nearly fully densified and show neither cracking nor warpage. After a subsequent silicide coating, the oxidation resistance of the 3D‐printed part is very significantly improved, which is a key step to making 3D‐printed RHEA structures useful at high temperatures.
